opus-5.5.text:
I think they're closely related, but they're not the same thing.

Reasoning ability is a foundation. If you look at what an Agent actually does, it has to break a goal into steps, decide which tool to call, read the result, notice when something went wrong, and adjust. Every one of those steps is a form of reasoning. So when a model gets better at long chains of thought, at reflection and self-correction, you generally see Agent performance go up as well. In a sense, an Agent is reasoning extended into the external world. Instead of only thinking inside its own context, the model now thinks, acts, gets feedback from the environment, and thinks again.

But I'd emphasize that strong reasoning alone doesn't automatically produce a strong Agent. There are a few gaps.

The first is long-horizon stability. A math problem might take a few thousand tokens of thinking, but a real Agent task can take dozens or hundreds of steps of interaction. The model has to keep the goal in mind, handle noisy or unexpected tool outputs, and not drift. That's a different kind of robustness from solving a single hard problem.

The second is interaction with the environment. In pure reasoning, all the information is in the prompt. In Agent settings, the model has to decide what information it's missing and go get it, by searching, running code, or browsing. Knowing when to stop thinking and start acting is itself a skill, and it isn't fully captured by reasoning benchmarks.

The third is training. I think the most important change is that we can now use reinforcement learning on end-to-end Agent tasks, letting the model actually use tools during training and learn from outcomes. That shapes behavior in ways that are hard to get from training on static reasoning data. So you could say reasoning gives you the capacity, and Agentic training teaches the model to turn that capacity into reliable action.

So my view is roughly this: reasoning is a necessary condition, and it sets the ceiling. Whether you reach that ceiling in real tasks depends on whether the model has learned to operate in a loop with the environment over long horizons. Going forward, I think the two will merge more and more. The best reasoning will happen through interaction, and the distinction between "thinking" and "acting" will become less important than whether the model can complete the task.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning is a necessary condition for Agent performance and sets its ceiling. It does not say strong Agents can perform well without correspondingly strong reasoning.

r002.rationale: The response links better long-chain reasoning with improved Agent performance, but does not state that solving the most complex tasks requires very strong reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two are much more tightly coupled than people often assume. When we talk about an Agent, we mean a model that can take on a long-horizon task, break it into steps, call tools, observe results, and adjust. Every one of those steps is actually a reasoning problem. Deciding what to do next, judging whether a tool's output is trustworthy, noticing that a plan has gone wrong and recovering from it, that is all reasoning. So I would say reasoning is the foundation, and Agent capability is what happens when you stretch that reasoning out over time and give it hands to act in the world.

The way I think about it is this: reasoning determines the quality of each individual decision, and Agent performance is the compounding of many such decisions. If a model's reasoning is slightly weak, in a single-turn setting you might barely notice. But in a thirty-step or hundred-step task, small errors accumulate. One wrong judgment early on, and everything downstream is built on a mistaken premise. That is why models that look similar on short benchmarks can diverge dramatically on long Agent tasks. The long horizon acts like a magnifying glass on reasoning quality.

But I also want to push back a little on the idea that it is purely one-directional. The Agent setting feeds back into reasoning. When a model has to act and then see real consequences, through code execution, search results, a failed test, that gives it a much richer signal than purely thinking in its head. Verification is the key word here. Reasoning without the ability to check yourself can go very far in the wrong direction while still sounding confident. An Agent that can run its ideas against reality has an external ground truth, and that ground truth is exactly what reinforcement learning needs. So in our own work, we have found that training in Agentic environments actually improves the model's underlying reasoning, not just its tool use. The model learns to be more careful, to form hypotheses it can actually test, to recognize when it does not know something.

So I would summarize it this way. Reasoning is the engine, the Agent framework is the vehicle, and long-horizon tasks with real feedback are the road that trains both. If you only optimize reasoning on static problems, you get a model that is clever but brittle when it meets the messy world. If you only optimize Agent scaffolding without strengthening reasoning, you get something that looks busy but makes poor decisions. The real progress comes from treating them as one problem, and I think that is where the frontier is right now.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning and Agent performance are tightly coupled and calls reasoning the foundation of Agent capability; it does not say strong Agent performance can occur without correspondingly strong reasoning.

r002.rationale: The response says every step in a long-horizon Agent task is a reasoning problem, that errors compound over many steps, and that Agent scaffolding without stronger reasoning leads to poor decisions.

astra-6.text:
I think reasoning is a foundation for Agent performance, but it isn’t the whole picture. Reasoning helps a model break down a goal, decide what to do next, and judge whether a result makes sense. An Agent has to turn those judgments into actions, observe what happens, and adjust its plan.

So the two are closely related, but stronger reasoning doesn’t automatically translate into a better Agent. A model might solve a clearly defined problem very well, yet struggle when it needs to find missing information, use tools, or recover from a failed action. And over a long task, small mistakes can accumulate.

What matters is whether reasoning works inside that action-and-feedback loop. Can the model recognize that its approach isn’t working? Can it verify that it actually completed the task? I’d look at reasoning ability as an important foundation, and Agent performance as a broader test of whether the model can use that ability reliably in an environment.

r001.rationale: The response says stronger reasoning does not automatically produce better Agent performance. That does not establish that strong Agent performance can occur without correspondingly strong reasoning; it also calls reasoning a foundation.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that solving the most complex tasks requires very strong reasoning ability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reasoning ability is a core foundation for Agent performance, but it’s only one part of the picture. An Agent has to turn an objective into actions, observe what happens, and adjust. Reasoning helps it decide what to do next, recognize when an approach has failed, and work out how to recover.

But stronger reasoning doesn’t automatically translate into a better Agent. The model also needs to use tools reliably, retain the right context, and keep working toward the objective over many steps. A model might solve a difficult, self-contained problem yet struggle when information is incomplete or an action produces an unexpected result.

So I see a feedback loop between the two. Better reasoning makes more complex Agent tasks possible, while training on Agent tasks can develop reasoning that is grounded in actions and feedback. Ultimately, we should evaluate whether the system can finish the task reliably, and how much time and computation it needs to do that.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning is a core foundation and that stronger reasoning does not automatically produce a better Agent. It does not state that strong Agent performance can be achieved without correspondingly strong reasoning.

r002.rationale: The response says better reasoning makes more complex Agent tasks possible, but does not say that solving the most complex tasks requires very strong reasoning.
